name: Lash extensions
lead: Lash extensions are individual synthetic (or sometimes natural-material) lashes attached by a technician to a person's own lashes with semi-permanent adhesive, to add length, curl and fullness. According to Wikipedia, an application typically takes up to two hours and lasts about three to four weeks depending on care.[1]
Styles are commonly described as classic (the most natural), volume (the fullest) and hybrid (a mix). The technician customises material, length, colour and curvature to the client's eyes.[1]
The adhesives commonly contain cyanoacrylate, and published case reports have linked the fumes to occupational asthma and rhinitis in lash technicians.[2]
infobox: Varies by US state; some require cosmetology or lash-specific licences[1]

paras: Artificial lashes predate extensions. Karl Nessler patented artificial lashes in the UK in 1902 to 1903 and sold them at his London salon, and Anna Taylor patented false eyelashes in the US in 1911. False lashes became popular in the early 1930s, and Twiggy helped popularise the doll-like lash look in the 1960s.[1] Magnetic false lashes were invented by Katy Stoka in 2014.[1]

Extensions are bonded to individual natural lashes using instant glue. Specialist equipment exists for the work, including a patented hands-free low-pressure air source with a finger-mounted nozzle, designed to dry or direct airflow during lash extension application.[3]

A 2013 report in Occupational Medicine described a case of occupational asthma with rhinitis and a case of rhinitis attributed to cyanoacrylate-based lash extension glue among beauty professionals, and evaluated respiratory exposure during lash extension work.[2] The authors noted that the number of practitioners was increasing with the service's popularity.[2]
Wikipedia notes that magnetic lashes may pose a hazard in MRI scanning rooms.[1]
No studies found on the effect of lash extensions on appearance. Published literature includes a case report of occupational respiratory disease in technicians exposed to the adhesive.[2]

In the United States each state regulates lash extension work, with some requiring a cosmetology or esthetician licence and others a separate lash-technician licence. In the UK, the Guild of Professional Beauty Therapists accredits courses on safe application.[1]

card.note: Adhesive fumes have been linked to respiratory problems in technicians.

quick.overview:
Lash extensions are individual false lashes glued onto natural lashes by a technician. They add length, curl and density and last roughly three to four weeks.

Styles range from natural-looking classic sets to fuller volume sets.
quick.mechanism: Each synthetic lash is attached to a single natural lash with cyanoacrylate-type adhesive, and falls out as the natural lash sheds.
quick.risks: A case report linked the glue to occupational asthma and rhinitis in technicians. Licensing rules vary by jurisdiction. Few clinical studies examine client outcomes.
